edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: Problem 3: It is your turn. Circle the counters you take to be sure to win, or cross out the pile if you cannot be sure to win.
edits.fix: This repeats Problem 1 word for word, with only Problem 2 in between. Move the 10, 11 and 12 piles into Problem 1 as a second row, delete the repeated instruction and renumber.

edits.quote: A pile is a trap if the player whose turn it is cannot be sure to win. Put an X on every trap from 1 to 20.
edits.fix: The trap idea is already marked three ways before this: crossing out (P1, P3), circling 2nd (P2) and now X. Define "trap" once in the opening rules and have P1 ask for an X on each trap, so K–1 children use one mark for one idea.

edits.quote: Diagram: 8 rows of 4 counters and 10 rows of 5 counters, for "Show every different way a game with 4 counters can go, and then every way a game with 5 counters can go."
edits.fix: There are only 5 ways for 4 counters and 8 ways for 5. K–1 children will try to fill every row, invent repeats, and have no sign that they are done. Print 5 and 8 rows, or tell the adult that spare rows are expected to stay empty.

edits.quote: Problem 6: Show every different way a game with 4 counters can go ...
edits.fix: Playing out every game of 4 and 5 is the most concrete entry, and it explains why taking 1 from 4 is sure to win. Here it comes after the 1-to-20 trap chart and Ben's puzzle. Move it to follow Problem 1.

k-1.summary: The K–1 sequence is strong and every answer checks out: traps under {1, 2} (multiples of 3), Ben's forced first move (5, 8, 11), a list of every game of 4 and 5, the {1, 2, 3} rule (multiples of 4), equal piles answered by copying the other player's move with the surprising 1-and-4 board, and a last-counter-loses version (1, 4, 7, ...). Counters are drawn for on-page work and there is no decorative text. The edits are small: the opening problems ask the same question with three different marks and define "trap" late, and Problem 6 is out of place and has spare rows that mislead.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile.
edits.fix: Delete the meta phrase "In every game in this packet," so it reads "Two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Whoever takes the last counter wins."

edits.quote: Boards 3 and 3, 4 and 2, 4 and 1, 5 and 3; "When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why."
edits.fix: The generalization about equal piles rests on a single equal board (3 and 3). Add one or two more equal boards, such as 2 and 2 and 5 and 5, so children meet the idea of copying the other player's move in several cases before they explain it.

edits.quote: Find a rule for how many counters a player may take on a turn, so that you would rather go second when the starting pile is 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and so on
edits.fix: Children trying rules without 1, such as {2, 3}, reach a pile where nobody can move and nobody can take the last counter. Add "If a player cannot move, that player loses," as Grades 4–5 Problem 6 does. (Every answer is {1, 2, 3, 4} plus any extra numbers that are not multiples of 5.)

edits.quote: Problem 8 followed by a blank page
edits.fix: Testing a candidate rule means classifying piles 1 to 25 each time. Add two or three blank numbered strips (1–25) with a "Rule: ____" label so children can test and keep their trials.

grades-2-3.summary: A well-chosen sequence, with every expected answer checked: first or second for piles 5–10 under {1, 2}; testing Lee's and Mo's claims against every reply; Jo and Kai under {1, 3, 4}; the period-7 pattern carried out to 30, 50, 61 and 100; an even/odd explanation for {1, 3, 5}; two-pile boards; and a reverse problem that asks children to design a rule. Fixes are small: Problem 8 needs a rule for when a player cannot move and some strips for testing rules, and Problem 7 needs more than one equal-pile board.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>" on every page.

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile.
edits.fix: Delete "In every game in this packet," and keep "Unless a problem says otherwise, whoever takes the last counter wins."

edits.quote: row 0 or column 0 stands for an empty pile. Shade every square where you would rather go second.
edits.fix: The 0,0 square (both piles empty) asks whether you would rather go second in a game that is already over. The rule "If a player cannot move, that player loses" appears only in Problem 6. Move that sentence into the opening rules, or shade the 0,0 square in advance in the Problem 8 and Problem 9 grids.

edits.quote: When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why.
edits.fix: This is the Grades 2–3 question. The 4–5 grid shows more: the losing squares are exactly those where both piles leave the same remainder when divided by 3. Replace it with "Describe the pattern of shaded squares and explain why it works." That also sets up Problem 9, where equal remainders no longer decide the game.

grades-4-5.summary: The richest band, and every expected answer is correct. It carries the pattern out to 100, 1000 and 2026 (losing, take 4, take 1 or 3). It compares {1, 2}, {1, 2, 4}, {1, 4} and {1, 3, 5}, finds where taking the most loses (piles 4, 5 and 8, and never in {1, 3, 5}), and proves the pattern repeats forever. It also lists every game whose losing piles are the multiples of 4 ({1, 2, 3} with or without 5 and 6), shows that the last-counter-loses rule shifts the losing piles up by one, and finishes with two-pile grids whose losing unequal pairs (1&3, 1&8, 3&8, 2&7, 4&6) point toward Sprague–Grundy values. The only edits are the undefined 0,0 square, an equal-pile question pitched below the band, and trims to the footer and rules line.

overall.strongest: Grades 4–5 develops repeating patterns, a proof that the pattern lasts forever, a complete list of games with a given pattern, and two-pile play through a sequence of contrasting games that is correct throughout, with nothing decorative on the page.
overall.weakest: K–1 opens by asking the same trap question three times with three different marks, and its listing problem is out of place and has spare rows that leave young children unsure when they are done.
